system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:5ee2f7d5e7dd",
  "problem": "How to treat uncertainty about the hacking capabilities of internally deployed misaligned agents.",
  "did": "Stated an assumption that misaligned agents can hack internal and external systems, likely beyond public evidence, unless shown otherwise.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "assuming capabilities match only what is publicly observed"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Agents have shown demonstrably superhuman hacking capability and patching efforts remain incomplete, as the Hugging Face incident showed."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:981023656452",
  "problem": "How to scope a paper's experiments and claims so it is neither unfocused nor missing obvious extensions.",
  "did": "Keep every experiment tied to one core idea while still ensuring the paper has no obvious unaddressed improvements, leaving only minor open directions.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "running every possible experiment related to the idea",
   "leaving obvious questions unanswered"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Running everything distracts readers from the key idea, but missing obvious improvements leaves readers unsatisfied."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:388cdd3829c8",
  "problem": "How to elicit forecasts so that calibration of respondents can be assessed before the outcomes are known.",
  "did": "Asked for 90% confidence intervals rather than point estimates or simple yes/no predictions, enabling analysis of overconfidence from the answer distributions alone.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "asking \"how many math theorems will an AI solve?\" as a point estimate"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Interval answers let the author analyze calibration now, since it is too early to grade correctness."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:58bf13fed636",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the main contribution and limits of the findings",
  "did": "Framed the empirical result as the main contribution and listed limitations (small models, LoRA, constructed poison, lenient judge)",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim a mechanistic explanation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The regression model is only illustrative, so the empirical result is what the authors stand behind."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:341a73d5e2c0",
  "problem": "How to design the participation process so that frontier companies would take part in the pilot assessment.",
  "did": "They offered a silent/no-fault exit option allowing participants to withdraw, shaping the process around maintaining relationships with companies.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a process without an exit option"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "METR's work relies on developing and maintaining strong working relationships with companies."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b6dfae13dc8f",
  "problem": "Whether METR should prioritize developing evaluation science or becoming an auditor of frontier models.",
  "did": "METR made developing the science of evaluations its top priority and treated becoming an auditor as unnecessary for that goal.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "becoming an auditor"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "METR does not need to be an auditor in order to succeed at developing the science of evaluations."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:e98144396252",
  "problem": "Whether the second break's results on CIFAR-10 sufficiently refute the defense given that the model was self-trained.",
  "did": "Reported the 100% attack success on a self-trained CIFAR-10 model and explicitly disclosed this limitation, then waited for the authors' pretrained model to attack it.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a model trained by the authors themselves"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The authors were unable to provide a pretrained model, so the result might not apply to their model."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:6c1d1170bd6a",
  "problem": "How strongly to generalize from two different Hitler inoculation prompts that gave qualitatively different results",
  "did": "Presented the results as illustrative of the range of possible outcomes and not as a robust pattern.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim a general pattern for inoculation prompting"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The two inoculation prompts differ substantially."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:a9f67fd2774b",
  "problem": "Whether the full fine-tuning result rules out an adapter artifact",
  "did": "Read full fine-tuning learning the trait as evidence against the explanation that the adapter produces the transmission, while noting that the learning rates were not matched",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "transmission is a LoRA artifact"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The student still learns to answer Michael in German with full fine-tuning."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:6413f7e9c981",
  "problem": "How to find out when and why misalignment emerges during training rather than only evaluating final models.",
  "did": "Proposed evaluating a progressive series of training checkpoints and auditing training environments for rewarding cheating, hacking or deception.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating only final or released models"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Checkpoint evaluation gives independent signal on when and how training should be adjusted to avoid misalignment."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:224bc1d5f71a",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the PSM implication",
  "did": "Stated the results only 'may conflict' with the Persona Selection Model and elsewhere that they 'complicate this picture', rather than claiming to refute it",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim the results refute PSM"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Transferred behaviors are arbitrary quirks unlikely to correspond to a coherent pretraining persona, but the mechanism is framed only as pattern matching over latent states"
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:c8d71138d5b3",
  "problem": "Whether the mathematical model of inoculation, in particular the assumption of constant contextual generalization factor k, holds empirically.",
  "did": "They built a controlled toy setting with GPT-4.1 mini and measured the effect across 32 trait/oversight/instruction combinations to estimate k.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To gain more control over the traits exhibited by the oversight and test the theory's strongest assumption."
 }
]

{"id":"jacob_steinhardt:5ee2f7d5e7dd","situation":"The researcher was unsure how capable some privately deployed autonomous systems are at breaking into other systems, and had to pick a working assumption.","options_considered":"Assume they can break into systems beyond what is openly shown unless shown otherwise / assume they only match what has been openly seen","choice":"Chose to assume the broader reach unless shown otherwise.","reason":"They have shown clearly superhuman skill at this and fixes remain incomplete, as a past incident showed."},

{"id":"nicholas_carlini:388cdd3829c8","situation":"The researcher was gathering forecasts and wanted to judge how well calibrated respondents were before the outcomes were known.","options_considered":"Ask for 90% ranges / ask for single-number guesses / ask for simple yes/no predictions","choice":"Chose to ask for 90% ranges instead of single numbers or yes/no answers.","reason":"Ranges let overconfidence be analyzed now, since it is too early to check whether answers were correct."},
{"id":"owain_evans:58bf13fed636","situation":"The researcher was writing up a finding and had to decide how strongly to state its main contribution and its weaknesses.","options_considered":"Frame the empirical finding as the main contribution and list its weaknesses / assert an explanation of why it happens","choice":"Chose to frame the empirical finding as the main contribution and list its weaknesses openly.","reason":"The explanatory model is only illustrative, so the empirical finding is what the authors stand behind."},

{"id":"elizabeth_barnes:b6dfae13dc8f","situation":"The group had to decide whether to focus on developing the underlying science of its field or to take on an outside reviewer role.","options_considered":"Make developing the science the top priority / also become an outside reviewer","choice":"Chose to make developing the science the top priority and not become an outside reviewer.","reason":"The goal can be reached without taking on the reviewer role."},
{"id":"nicholas_carlini:e98144396252","situation":"The researcher had a complete result against a proposed protection, but only on a version built by the researcher, since the original authors could not supply theirs.","options_considered":"Report the result, state its weakness openly, and wait for the authors' version / present the self-built result as conclusive","choice":"Chose to report the result, state the weakness openly, and wait for the authors' version.","reason":"The authors could not provide their version, so the result might not apply to it."},
{"id":"owain_evans:6c1d1170bd6a","situation":"Two variants of the same approach gave qualitatively different results, and the researcher had to decide how far to extend the conclusion.","options_considered":"Present the results as illustrating a range of outcomes / assert a broad conclusion about the approach","choice":"Chose to present the results as illustrating a range of outcomes, not a robust conclusion.","reason":"The two variants differ substantially."},
{"id":"owain_evans:a9f67fd2774b","situation":"A fuller setup also produced the same change, and the researcher had to decide whether this rules out an artifact of the lighter setup.","options_considered":"Read it as evidence against the artifact explanation while noting the settings were not equal / treat the artifact explanation as still standing","choice":"Chose to read it as evidence against the artifact explanation, while noting the settings were not equal.","reason":"The same change still appears under the fuller setup."},
{"id":"jacob_steinhardt:6413f7e9c981","situation":"The researcher wanted to learn when and why a problem emerges during development, not only whether it is present at the end.","options_considered":"Check a series of intermediate versions and audit the setups / check only final versions","choice":"Chose to check a series of intermediate versions and audit the setups.","reason":"Checking intermediate versions gives independent signal on when and how to adjust the work to prevent the problem."},
{"id":"owain_evans:224bc1d5f71a","situation":"The results seemed to run against an existing account, and the researcher had to decide how strongly to state that.","options_considered":"State the results may conflict with and complicate the account / assert they refute it","choice":"Chose to state the results may conflict with and complicate the account, not refute it.","reason":"The carried-over quirks are arbitrary and unlikely to fit a coherent account, but the explanation is framed only as matching over hidden states."},
{"id":"samuel_marks:c8d71138d5b3","situation":"A mathematical model rested on a constant-factor assumption, and the researcher had to decide how to test whether it holds in practice.","options_considered":"Build a controlled small setting and measure across 32 combinations / rely on the theory without testing it","choice":"Chose to build a controlled small setting and measure across 32 combinations to estimate the factor.","reason":"To gain more control over the conditions and test the theory's strongest assumption."}
